content: Acetaminophen injection is an analgesic and antipyretic medication approved by the FDA for the treatment of pain and fever. It is important to note that exceeding the recommended dosage can lead to severe hepatic injury, including liver failure and death. The maximum daily dose includes all sources of acetaminophen, whether administered orally, rectally, or intravenously. For adults and adolescents weighing 50 kg or more, the recommended dose is 1000 mg every 6 hours or 650 mg every 4 hours, with a maximum single dose of 1000 mg and a maximum daily dose of 4000 mg. For patients under 50 kg, the dose is weight-based, with a maximum daily dose of 75 mg/kg. Acetaminophen infusion should be administered intravenously over 15 minutes, and the vial contents must be inspected for particulate matter or discoloration before use. The drug should not be mixed with other medications in the same infusion device. Acetaminophen is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to the drug or its excipients and in those with severe hepatic impairment or active liver disease. It should be used cautiously in patients with renal impairment, and dose adjustments may be necessary. Rare but serious skin reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported. Patients should discontinue the drug immediately if signs of hypersensitivity or skin rash occur. In clinical trials, common adverse reactions included nausea, vomiting, headache, and insomnia. Pediatric patients experienced similar adverse events, with additional reports of pruritus, agitation, and atelectasis. Acetaminophen infusion has been studied in pediatric populations, but its safety and efficacy in children under 2 years of age have not been established. During pregnancy, acetaminophen should only be used if clearly needed, as there are no adequate studies on intravenous administration in pregnant women. However, epidemiological data on oral acetaminophen use during pregnancy do not indicate an increased risk of major congenital malformations. Acetaminophen is excreted in breast milk in small amounts, and caution is advised when administering it to nursing mothers. The pharmacokinetics of acetaminophen infusion have been studied across various age groups, showing dose proportionality in adults and higher exposure in neonates and infants. The drug is primarily metabolized in the liver through glucuronidation, sulfation, and oxidation pathways, with metabolites excreted in the urine. In cases of overdose, acetaminophen can cause dose-dependent, potentially fatal hepatic necrosis. Early symptoms include nausea, vomiting, and malaise, with hepatic toxicity becoming evident 48 to 72 hours post-ingestion. Treatment involves prompt administration of the antidote N-acetylcysteine (NAC) and monitoring of liver function. Acetaminophen infusion is supplied in 100 mL glass vials containing 1000 mg of the drug. It is intended for single use, and any unused portion must be discarded.
